Issued at 233 AM MDT Wed Oct 14 2026

The main driver in the forecast this morning remains me of one of 
the better movies of the mid 1990s, Leaving Las Vegas. It is 
because the upper level low that has brought the clouds and 
showers of the past few days that was centered near Las Vegas is
now leaving and will be making a turn toward to the northeast, 
crossing Colorado through tonight before moving into the central
Plains states for the end of the week. And it will continue be 
the main driver in the weather for about the next 24 to 36 
hours. 

Satellite imagery shows some more enhanced cloud tops heading toward 
Wyoming, with showers across much of the southern two thirds of the 
area. There remains some uncertainty this morning in regards to how 
widespread the showers will be today though. Some ensemble members, 
as well as the operational GFS, keep the low further south, keeping 
more of the area mainly dry, with showers confined largely south and 
west of a Buffalo to Riverton to Green River line. Other members, as 
well as the operational European model, bring the low closer and 
keep showers across most of the southern two thirds of the area 
through this evening. There is some agreement in showers starting to 
end from northwest to southeast starting after midnight tonight, 
with all showers finally over by noon on Thursday. 

Now we turn to precipitation amounts. Far northwestern Wyoming 
should be done with showers. As for an additional quarter of an inch 
starting at 6 am this morning, the 1 out of 2 chance of an 
additional quarter inch or more runs roughly south and east of a 
Kaycee to east of Riverton to Rock Springs line. However, 
precipitation has been underperforming in most locations. The 
heaviest amounts, with around a 2 out of 5 chance of three quarter 
inches of rain are mainly in Natrona, southeastern Fremont and 
southern Sweetwater Counties. 

And finally, we talk about snow. Amounts over the passes have been 
rather small so far. Snow levels will reach the lowest point early 
this morning. With 700 millibar temperatures generally dropping to 
between minus 2 to minus 3, which would lower snow levels to around 
7000 to 7500 feet. This would keep the lower elevations largely 
rain, although there could be some wet snowflakes from time to time, 
especially if precipitation is heavier. As for an additional inch 
starting at 6 am this morning, it mainly across the Wind River 
Range, the Green and Rattlesnake Ranges and also Casper Mountain 
where there is a greater than 1 in 2 chance of 1 inch or greater. 
When we bump it up to 3 inches, it is again mainly above 8500 feet. 
However, the NBM ensemble has a couple of interesting things. It 
still has a greater than 2 out of 5 chance of 3 inches over the 
higher elevations of South Pass. I am giving some thought to 
possibly extending the Winter Weather Advisory another 6 hours or 
so, when snow levels should rise another 1000 feet or so. This will 
likely be a gametime decision based on road conditions when we get 
closer to expiration, which is at 6 am. Other locations that 
could see over 3 inches include Casper Mountain, but all 
guidance keeps the chance of over 6 inches to less than 1 out of
5. The other location is the Green and Rattlesnake Range, but 
this would be the higher elevations with no impacts. Snow should
really taper off after midnight with just about all areas done 
by Thursday morning.

And you think we are done, but wait, there's more! And that will be 
the strong wind tonight. The upper level will initiate some lee 
cyclogenesis over Colorado and tighten the pressure gradient as the 
low deepens. This will be mainly after midnight tonight and into 
Thursday morning, although it will linger longer over Johnson 
County. Most areas East of the Divide as well as eastern Sweetwater 
County have at least a 3 out of 5 chance of wind gusts past 30 mph. 
The areas prone to the cold advection / north flow pattern, like 
Johnson County and portions of the Big Horn Basin have at least a 1 
in 2 chance of gusts past 40 mph. High wind looks unlikely, as 700 
millibar wind looks to top out at around 40 knots, and I would 
likely to see 50 knots for that. Wind should decrease Thursday 
afternoon as the low moves into the Plains states.

And this brings us to the last main concern, a possibly killing 
freeze. Yes, most locations are a few weeks past the average first 
freeze, so we have been living on borrowed time. But many areas will 
have a good chance Thursday night as the wind decreases and the sky 
the sky clears as the low moves away. Thursday night there is a very 
good chance of that killing freeze. Just about the entire area has 
at least a 2 out of 3 chance of temperatures of 28 degrees or below. 
Freeze warnings will likely be needed, but we will let future shifts 
issue these as we still have rain and snow to deal with.
